summary: Defines the acct URI scheme, which identifies a user's account at a service provider independent of which protocols are used to reach it. The form looks like an email address with an acct: prefix.

plainLanguage.summary: A name tag that says who you are at which service, without saying how to contact you.

questions: how to identify a user account with uri
what is the acct uri scheme
what does an acct uri look like
how is acct used in webfinger
subtitle: A URI scheme that names a user's account at a service, without saying how to talk to it.

tldr.problem: Existing URI schemes such as mailto and http tie an account to one service or protocol, and no scheme identified an account generically.
tldr.mechanism: The acct scheme takes the form acct:user@host, where the user part is the account name and the host is the DNS domain of the service provider. It identifies the account only; the protocol using it decides how to resolve it.
tldr.outcome: At the time of writing only WebFinger used it, and the scheme is not restricted to that protocol.

today: RFC 7565 is a Proposed Standard from May 2015. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Gap acct Fills
sections.content: URI schemes that identify or interact with a user's account are tied to particular services or protocols. The mailto scheme enables interaction with an email account, and the http scheme retrieves web files or interfaces about a user. No scheme generically identified a user's account at a service provider without naming a protocol to use. RFC 7565 defines the acct URI scheme to fill that gap.
sections.plainLanguage: There were ways to say "email me" or "visit my page", but no way to just say "this is my account here".

sections.title: Rationale from WebFinger
sections.content:
While the WebFinger protocol (RFC 7033) was being formalized, participants discussed which URI scheme should name a user's account in a web link. Both mailto (RFC 6068) and http (RFC 7230) were proposed. Neither fits every provider: a microblogging or instant messaging provider might not offer email, and an enterprise might not offer HTTP interfaces about its employees. So a scheme independent of application protocol was defined.

A user need not be human; it can be a bot or a role-based alias. An acct URI always identifies something that has an account at a service, never the service itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every place has a mailbox or a website, so they needed a name tag that works for everyone.

sections.title: How acct URIs Are Formed
sections.content:
An acct URI looks like user@host with the prefix acct:. The scheme is for identification, not interaction. The user part is the account name, and the host is the DNS domain name of the service provider. For an account named foobar on status.example.net, the URI is acct:foobar@status.example.net.

If the account name is itself an email address, the at-sign must be percent-encoded. A user with the address juliet@capulet.example registered at shoppingsite.example gets acct:juliet%40capulet.example@shoppingsite.example.

The RFC does not assume anyone can interact with the account using any protocol, even if the part after the scheme happens to work as an email address. It specifies no way to dereference an acct URI on its own, for example in an HTML href. Any protocol that uses acct URIs must define how they are resolved. With WebFinger, an application resolves the host to a WebFinger server and passes the URI in a request such as GET /.well-known/webfinger?resource=acct%3Abob%40example.com. To compare two acct URIs, an application MUST use the case normalization and percent-encoding normalization of RFC 3986, Sections 6.2.2.1 and 6.2.2.2.
sections.plainLanguage: Your tag reads "name at place". It tells people who you are there. If they want to write or visit, they have to pick the right method themselves.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since the scheme does not directly enable interaction with an account, direct security concerns are minimized. An acct URI does, however, prove that the account exists. Harvesting published acct URIs could help spammers and similar attackers, for example by using WebFinger to learn more or by using the same user@host in protocol-specific URIs such as mailto.

Protocols that use acct URIs must define their own security considerations. Percent-encoding allows a wider range of characters but adds risk, so implementers are advised to disallow encoded characters or sequences that would produce space, null, control or other forbidden characters, allow unauthorized access to private data, or cause other vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tag proves someone exists, which a bad person could use to pester them. So be careful who gets to see a list of tags.

sections.title: Internationalization
sections.content:
Following RFC 3986, any Unicode character can be used, encoded as UTF-8 and then percent-encoded into ASCII. Before percent-encoding, an application MUST ensure three things about its input:

  • the user part uses only code points allowed by the PRECIS IdentifierClass (RFC 7564);
  • the host uses only code points allowed by the rules in RFC 5892;
  • internationalized domain name labels are encoded as A-labels (RFC 5890).
sections.plainLanguage: Names with letters from any language are allowed, but they must first be turned into a safe plain-letter code, and only certain letters are allowed to start with.

sections.title: Syntax and IANA Registration
sections.content:
The RFC registers the scheme as acct with status permanent. Its syntax in ABNF is:

acctURI  = "acct" ":" userpart "@" host
userpart = unreserved / sub-delims
           0*( unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims )

No media type is associated with the scheme. The registration notes that only WebFinger used it at the time of writing, but use is not restricted to that protocol. It lists no known interoperability concerns, and the IETF holds change control.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for the name tag were written down in an official list so everyone builds the tags the same way.
